## Motivation

The earlier vignettes on amphibian disease combined two counts, uninfected and infected
frogs, into one number with a weight `w`. Choosing `w` is a value judgement, and the
analyst may not be the person to make it. The alternative is to keep the objectives
apart and report the *Pareto front*: the actions that are not beaten on every objective
at once by some other action. Anything off the front can be discarded whatever the
weight. What is on the front is the real menu.

This vignette computes the front for the two disease counts, relates it to the
weighted sum, and shows a case the weighted sum cannot find.

## The problem

A pond holds frogs, and Bd may be absent, present at low prevalence, or present at high
prevalence. Five actions are considered: no intervention, salt added to the pond,
antifungal baths, testing every frog and removing the infected ones, and draining and
disinfecting the pond. Two outcomes are counted two years from now:

- uninfected frogs alive (more is better);
- infected frogs alive (fewer is better).

Infected but living frogs are not counted as population in this series. They are a
separate count, to be kept low.

**All numbers are illustrative**, not data and not estimates for any real treatment.

```{julia}
using DecisionAnalysis
include(joinpath("..", "_common.jl"))
using Plots

actions = [:no_intervention, :salt, :antifungal_baths, :remove_infected, :disinfect_pond]
states = [:absent, :low_prevalence, :high_prevalence]
uninfected = PayoffTable(actions, states,
                         [500 300 100
                          490 320 160
                          470 380 250
                          480 330 200
                          350 340 320])
infected = PayoffTable(actions, states,
                       [0 150 250
                        0 120 200
                        0  60 120
                        0  50 100
                        0  10  20])
prior = FiniteBelief(states, [1 // 2, 3 // 10, 1 // 5])
uninfected
```

```{julia}
infected
```

## One table per objective

Every objective is a payoff table on the same actions and states, written so that
higher is better. The infected count is to be kept low, so its table is the count with
a minus sign: tables with the same labels can be negated, added, subtracted and
scaled. The objectives are a named collection of tables, and they share one belief.

```{julia}
objectives = (; more_uninfected=uninfected, fewer_infected=-infected)
```

Taken one at a time, each is an ordinary decision problem. No intervention is the
baseline of both.

```{julia}
more_uninfected = DecisionProblem(objectives.more_uninfected, prior;
                                  baseline=:no_intervention)
fewer_infected = DecisionProblem(objectives.fewer_infected, prior;
                                 baseline=:no_intervention)

md_table(["action", "expected uninfected", "gain over no intervention",
          "expected infected", "change from no intervention"],
         [[a, u, gu, -i, -gi]
          for (a, u, gu, i, gi) in zip(actions,
                                       aggregate(Expectation(), more_uninfected),
                                       expected_gain_over_baseline(more_uninfected),
                                       aggregate(Expectation(), fewer_infected),
                                       expected_gain_over_baseline(fewer_infected))])
```

Taken alone, the first objective chooses the baths and the second disinfection.

```{julia}
first_choice(decide(more_uninfected, MaxExpectedUtility())),
first_choice(decide(fewer_infected, MaxExpectedUtility()))
```

## The Pareto front

`decide(objectives, prior, ParetoFront())` scores every action on every objective (by
expectation unless another aggregator is given) and keeps the actions that are not
dominated. An action is dominated when another is at least as good on every objective
and strictly better on one. The result displays the scores, one column per objective,
and marks the front. The second column is minus the expected number infected, so that
higher is better in both.

```{julia}
front = decide(objectives, prior, ParetoFront(); baseline=:no_intervention)
```

```{julia}
front.chosen
```

No intervention and salt are off the front. The baths give more uninfected frogs *and*
fewer infected frogs than either, so no weight on the two counts could justify them.
That includes business as usual: here doing nothing is dominated.

```{julia}
x = Float64.(front.scores[:, 1])
y = Float64.(-front.scores[:, 2])
on = [a in front.chosen for a in front.actions]
plt = scatter(x[on], y[on]; label="on the Pareto front", markersize=7,
              xlabel="expected uninfected frogs (more is better)",
              ylabel="expected infected frogs (fewer is better)",
              title="Two objectives, five actions (illustrative)",
              legend=:bottomright, xlims=(330, 410), ylims=(-25, 110))
scatter!(plt, x[.!on], y[.!on]; label="dominated", markersize=7, markershape=:xcross)
ends = [findfirst(==(:disinfect_pond), actions), findfirst(==(:antifungal_baths), actions)]
plot!(plt, x[ends], y[ends]; label="reachable by a weighted sum", linestyle=:dash,
      color=:gray)
annotate!(plt, [(x[i] , y[i] + 6, text(String(a), 8)) for (i, a) in enumerate(actions)])
png_figure(plt)
```

The best corner of this figure is the bottom right: many uninfected, few infected. The
dashed line joins the two actions that a weighted sum can select, as shown below.

## The weighted sum and the front

The weighted problem of the earlier vignettes is utility = uninfected − `w` × infected.
For any `w ≥ 0` its best action is on the front. The sweep shows which.

```{julia}
function weighted(w)
    return DecisionProblem(infection_payoff(; uninfected, infected, weight=w), prior;
                           baseline=:no_intervention)
end

md_table(["w", "best action", "expected utility", "gain over no intervention"],
         [begin
              p = weighted(w)
              [exact(w), first_choice(decide(p, MaxExpectedUtility())), act_now_value(p),
               maximum(expected_gain_over_baseline(p))]
          end
          for w in (0, 1 // 2, 1, 3 // 2, 2, 3)])
```

```{julia}
ws = 0:(1 // 20):3
lines = [Float64(aggregate(Expectation(), weighted(w))[i])
         for w in ws, i in eachindex(actions)]
plt = plot(Float64.(ws), lines; label=permutedims(String.(actions)),
           xlabel="weight w on infected frogs",
           ylabel="expected uninfected − w × infected",
           title="Weighted sum against the weight (illustrative)")
png_figure(plt)
```

At `w = 0` and `w = 1` the baths are best. Disinfection takes over once an infected frog
counts for more than about 1.66 uninfected ones:

```{julia}
switch = findfirst(w -> first_choice(decide(weighted(w), MaxExpectedUtility())) ==
                        :disinfect_pond, ws)
exact(ws[switch])
```

The sweep steps in twentieths, so this is the first grid value at which disinfection
wins.

## What the weighted sum cannot find

Removing infected frogs is on the front and is never the best action for any weight.
Its line in the figure above is never the highest.

```{julia}
unique(first_choice(decide(weighted(w), MaxExpectedUtility())) for w in 0:(1 // 100):10)
```

It is a compromise that lies on the wrong side of the dashed line joining the baths and
disinfection in the scatter plot, and a weighted sum only ever picks out the points on
the outer hull of the front. A manager who wanted, say, at least 370 uninfected frogs
and at most 40 infected ones in expectation would choose it, and no value of `w` would
have offered it. Sweeping a weight is therefore not a substitute for computing the
front.

```{julia}
[a for (i, a) in enumerate(front.actions)
 if front.scores[i, 1] >= 370 && -front.scores[i, 2] <= 40]
```

## Other aggregators

`ParetoFront(aggregator)` scores the objectives with something other than the
expectation. With `WorstCase()` an action is judged on its worst state for each
objective, with no probabilities.

```{julia}
worst = decide(objectives, prior, ParetoFront(WorstCase()))
```

Judged on worst cases, disinfection is best on both objectives at once and the front
is a single action. The front depends on how each objective is summarised over the
states, and that choice should be stated with it.

The same call takes any number of objectives, for example one table per species when
a management action helps one species and harms another. The tables must share their
actions and states. Objectives that do not share a belief can still be compared: pass
a vector of `DecisionProblem`s, one per objective, to `decide(problems, ParetoFront())`.

## What to take away

- Write each objective as its own payoff table, with higher better, and pass the named
  collection and the belief to `decide(objectives, belief, ParetoFront())`.
- `infection_payoff(; uninfected, infected, weight)` is the weighted sum of the two
  counts, and tables with the same labels add, subtract and scale.
- Dominated actions can be dropped without choosing a weight. Here no intervention and
  salt are dominated by the baths.
- The best action of uninfected − `w` × infected is on the front for every `w ≥ 0`:
  baths for small `w`, disinfection for large `w`.
- The converse fails. Removing infected frogs is on the front and is not optimal for
  any `w`. A weight sweep finds only part of the front.
- Infected but living animals are a separate count to be minimised, not part of the
  population.
